payload.stem: A swimmer can swim at $2.5\text{ m/s}$ relative to still water and wants to reach the point directly opposite her starting point on the far bank of a river $100\text{ m}$ wide. The current is $1.5\text{ m/s}$ parallel to the banks. She heads upstream at the angle that makes her path perpendicular to the banks. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: Uses the swimming speed relative to the water, $w/v_s=40.0\text{ s}$, as if there were no current.
Uses the resultant speed $\sqrt{v_s^2+v_r^2}$ for the crossing, $w/\sqrt{v_s^2+v_r^2}=34.3\text{ s}$.
The speed across the river is $\sqrt{v_s^2-v_r^2}=2.00\text{ m/s}$, so $t=w/\sqrt{v_s^2-v_r^2}=50.0\text{ s}$.
Uses the sum of the speeds, $w/(v_s+v_r)=25.0\text{ s}$.

payload.title: Uniform rod released from the horizontal

stimulus.description: A uniform rod of mass $M=1\text{ kg}$ and length $L=1\text{ m}$ is held horizontal and is free to rotate about a frictionless horizontal pivot at one end. The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is $\tfrac13ML^2$. The rod is released from rest. Use $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the center of mass of the rod at the instant of release, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the rod. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from the dot: the weight straight down and the force of the pivot straight up (its magnitude is less than the weight because the center of mass accelerates downward).

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight (down) and the force exerted by the pivot (up), with no extra force such as a force of rotation
common_errors: adds a force of rotation
draws only the weight

rubric_rows.criterion: The directions are correct: weight straight down and the pivot force straight up
common_errors: draws the pivot force horizontal at the instant of release

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight arrow is longer than the pivot-force arrow because the center of mass accelerates downward
common_errors: draws equal lengths for an accelerating rod

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the angular acceleration $\alpha$ of the rod just after the release in terms of $g$ and $L$.
parts.model_answer: The torque of the weight about the pivot is $Mg(L/2)$, so $\alpha=\tau/I=Mg(L/2)/(\tfrac13ML^2)=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the torque of the weight about the pivot, $\tau=Mg(L/2)$, using the center of mass at $L/2$
common_errors: uses the lever arm L

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies $\tau=I\alpha$ with $I=\tfrac13ML^2$
common_errors: uses the rotational inertia about the center, $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $\alpha=3g/(2L)$ (the mass cancels)
common_errors: obtains $g/L$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the angular speed of the rod when it is vertical, for $L=1\text{ m}$.
parts.model_answer: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12(\tfrac13ML^2)\omega^2$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}\approx5.42\text{ rad/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Equates the loss of gravitational energy of the center of mass to the rotational kinetic energy: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12I\omega^2$
common_errors: uses the drop L for the center of mass

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 5.42 with units of radians per second

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A second rod of the same length but twice the mass is released in the same way. Does the angular acceleration just after the release increase, decrease or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It stays the same, because the torque $Mg(L/2)$ and the rotational inertia $\tfrac13ML^2$ are both proportional to $M$ and the mass cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the angular acceleration stays the same
common_errors: states that the angular acceleration doubles

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the mass appears in both the torque and the rotational inertia and cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$
common_errors: argues only that all objects fall at the same rate

payload.title: Perfectly inelastic collision of two carts

stimulus.description: A cart of mass $m_1=1\text{ kg}$ moves at $v=6\text{ m/s}$ on a frictionless horizontal track and collides with a stationary cart of mass $m_2=2\text{ kg}$. The carts stick together.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that both the total momentum and the total kinetic energy of the two carts are conserved in the collision. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The momentum is conserved because there is no external horizontal force on the carts, but the carts stick together, so the collision is perfectly inelastic and part of the kinetic energy is transformed into internal energy.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim (only the momentum is conserved)
common_errors: agrees that both are conserved

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the momentum is conserved because there is no external horizontal force on the system of the two carts
required_elements: no external force so momentum conserved
common_errors: says momentum is lost because the carts stick

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the kinetic energy is not conserved because the carts stick together (the collision is perfectly inelastic) and some energy becomes internal energy
common_errors: says the energy disappears without any transformation

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed of the combined carts after the collision and the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost, in terms of $m_1$ and $m_2$.
parts.model_answer: $m_1v=(m_1+m_2)v_f$ gives $v_f=m_1v/(m_1+m_2)=2.00\text{ m/s}$ and the lost fraction is $1-K_f/K_i=m_2/(m_1+m_2)=0.667$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies conservation of momentum: $m_1v=(m_1+m_2)v_f$
common_errors: conserves the kinetic energy instead

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_f=m_1v/(m_1+m_2)$
common_errors: puts $m_2$ in the numerator

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains the lost fraction $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ from $K_f/K_i=m_1/(m_1+m_2)$
common_errors: gives the fraction that remains

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The stationary cart is replaced by one with twice the mass, $4\text{ kg}$. Does the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost increase, decrease or stay the same? Give its new value and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It increases to $2m_2/(m_1+2m_2)=0.800$, because the lost fraction $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ increases with $m_2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the lost fraction increases to about 0.800
common_errors: states that the fraction is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$, which increases with $m_2$ (a heavier target makes the final speed smaller and the loss larger)
common_errors: argues only that heavier objects lose more energy

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed of the combined carts after the collision and the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost, in terms of $m_1$ and $m_2$.
parts.model_answer: $m_1v=(m_1+m_2)v_f$ gives $v_f=m_1v/(m_1+m_2)=2.00\text{ m/s}$ and the lost fraction is $1-K_f/K_i=m_2/(m_1+m_2)=0.333$.

parts.prompt: The stationary cart is replaced by one with twice the mass, $2\text{ kg}$. Does the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost increase, decrease or stay the same? Give its new value and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It increases to $2m_2/(m_1+2m_2)=0.500$, because the lost fraction $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ increases with $m_2$.

difficulty.label: exam_prep
difficulty.rationale: Standard perfectly inelastic collision. Part A requires choosing the governing law (momentum conserved, KE not, since the carts stick together). Part B is a short symbolic derivation giving v' = m1 v/(m1+m2) and a KE loss fraction of m2/(m1+m2). Part C is one proportional-reasoning step (loss fraction goes from 1/3 to 1/2, so it increases) that links the result to a claim. Reading and arithmetic loads are minimal and the wording is unambiguous. Concepts are in scope, and difficulty comes only from legitimate levers (law selection, symbolic derivation, one reasoning-to-claim step). It is at the easier end of exam_prep.
